items.title: Mesh LLM launches distributed AI computing platform using iroh to pool GPUs across machines with OpenAI-compatible API [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Mesh LLM: distributed AI computing on iroh
items.summary:
Mesh LLM introduces a distributed AI computing system that pools GPUs and memory from multiple machines to run large language models without relying on centralized data centers or metered APIs. It exposes a single OpenAI-compatible API endpoint, allowing users to start with one node and scale by adding more, with the system deciding whether to run models locally, route to peers, or split models across machines.

The platform uses iroh endpoints on each node to establish secure, authenticated QUIC connections with NAT traversal and relay fallback, enabling direct peer-to-peer communication without a central server. Mesh LLM supports over 40 models, including large mixture-of-experts models partitioned across nodes, and offers both public and private deployment options. A mobile app is planned to extend mesh participation using emerging agent standards.

items.title: Political Neutrality Benchmark finds 97 of 108 AI model positions lean left of center across six political dimensions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Political Neutrality Benchmark of popular AI models
items.summary:
A new benchmark analyzing eighteen AI models from twelve labs across four regions reveals that 97 out of 108 measured political positions lean left of center, with xAI's Groks models near the center. The study assesses models on six political dimensions using each model's self-anchored scale and notes that some models, including Phi-4, declined a significant portion of questions, affecting their neutrality scores.

The benchmark provides interactive visualizations mapping models by overall political leaning and intelligence scores, and it allows ongoing contributions from the community to expand the dataset. The results emphasize relative positioning within each model's own political spectrum rather than absolute measures, and caution is advised when interpreting models that refused many questions or belong to families involved in the benchmark's reference data.

items.title: Open-AGS releases Attestor, a zero trust boundary system for AI agent operations with policy checks and customer-owned enforcement gates [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Show HN: Zero Trust Boundary for Agents
items.summary:
Open-AGS has released Attestor, a zero trust boundary system designed to control high-risk AI-driven operations by verifying policy, authority, scope, and evidence before execution. Attestor acts as an intermediary between AI-prepared operations and execution systems, providing decisions such as admit, narrow, review, or block, and records the rationale for each decision to ensure accountability.

Attestor supports integration with existing APIs and tools, offering a shadow pilot mode to observe potential risks before enforcement. It emphasizes customer ownership of the enforcement gate to ensure that only approved actions proceed, addressing risks from hallucinations, stale context, or hostile content. The system aligns with frameworks like the EU AI Act and NIST AI Risk Management Framework but does not claim compliance. The current release is an evaluation baseline intended for local review and integration planning, with live deployment and security audits planned separately.

items.title: Maker builds Unify AI Horn alternative using ESP32, WizNet 5500 Ethernet, PoE, and TI Class-D amplifier for weatherproof audio announcements [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Unify AI Horn alternative using ESP32, WizNet 5500, Poe and a Ti Amp
items.summary:
A maker designed and built a weatherproof audio announcement system as an alternative to the Ubiquiti UniFi AI Horn, using an ESP32-S3 microcontroller, WizNet W5500 Ethernet controller, ST PM8805 PoE controller, and a Texas Instruments TAS5760L Class-D amplifier. The device supports both Wi-Fi and wired Ethernet, runs custom firmware with a web interface for audio upload and configuration, and uses an SD card for local audio storage to ensure announcements function even if the server is unreachable.

The project was motivated by the need to deter deer damaging a garden, triggered by UniFi camera AI animal detection webhooks. The custom PCB was designed in KiCad and manufactured in China, with the assembled units housed in weatherproof enclosures and connected via a single PoE cable. While the system works reliably, the deer eventually ignored the announcements, though the device has proven useful for other unwanted visitors.

items.title: Researchers develop AgenticSTS AI with structured memory layers that wins 6 out of 10 games in Slay the Spire 2, outperforming agents using growing chat logs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AI agents win at Slay the Spire 2 after researchers replace growing chat logs with structured memory
items.summary:
Researchers from Alaya Lab and Shanghai Jiao Tong University created AgenticSTS, an AI agent that replaces expanding chat logs with five structured memory layers to manage information during gameplay. Tested on the card game Slay the Spire 2, the agent maintains a prompt size of about 5,000 tokens instead of hundreds of thousands and achieves a 60% win rate at the lowest difficulty, while competing agents failed to win any games.

AgenticSTS organizes memory into fixed protocol instructions, state schemas, game rules, past run summaries, and strategy skills, allowing it to efficiently rebuild decisions without carrying an ever-growing chat history. The inclusion of a skill library doubled the agent's win rate compared to setups without it. The approach also significantly reduces token usage and model latency compared to other agents that resend the entire game history with each move.

The researchers note that memory contents are model-specific and do not transfer well between different AI models. While the results demonstrate improved performance and efficiency, further testing is needed to isolate the effects of the memory architecture within the same codebase and across more runs and difficulty levels.

The proxy model pattern changes the traditional database-to-LLM interaction, enabling faster, cost-effective AI-powered querying within standard SQL workflows.
